Greener On The Other Side

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We travel to Europe's greenest city and ask: What's stopping South Africa's towns from cleaning up their act?

Unique Selling Point:
Sweden's Vaxjo claims to be Europe's greenest city. It is carbon neutral, runs its transport network on recycled waste and uses the latest construction techniques to limit the environmental impact of its own expansion. This will be a first-hand view of the type of future all cities should aspire to, and provides the prefect yardstick against which to measure South Africa's cities and towns.

Summary:
This is a story about the type of green future that is possible with a little foresight, planning and political will. Vaxjo is a shining light in a country that has made clear its intention to unburden itself of fossil fuels within the next few years. So precise has its vision become, that it even takes steps to mitigate the environmental impact of modern construction methods. We will be taken on a tour of the city and shown the initiatives and technologies that have made it Europe's greenest.

But, this is also a story about a country that is being left behind in the race for carbon neutrality. South Africa is still largely reliant on fossil fuels and one of its provinces holds the inglorious title as the world's most polluted. Recent satellite imagery highlighted alarming levels of Nitrogen Di Oxide in the atmosphere - a direct consequence of the province's positioning at the centre of coal-fired energy provision. It is the antithesis of Vaxjo.

Vested interests, misunderstanding, misdirection and fear have all contributed to a widespread distrust of clean energy and its independent producers. So, can South Africa produce its own Vaxjo? And, if not, what will the consequence be of a failure to convince Eskom, the mines and the unions that this is the only way forward?

Press Release:


Greener on the Other Side
Late last year, the analysis of satellite data showing air pollution around the world revealed that the coal town of Emalahleni in Mpumalanga is the largest nitrogen dioxide hotspot across six continents. With the World Health Organisation estimating that seven million people around the world die from air pollution every year, what can local government do to respond to the public health crisis? Carte Blanche travelled from the town with the dirtiest air in the world, to Vaxjo in Sweden, a town striving to be the greenest in Europe, to learn how South Africa, can clean up its air pollution.
Producer & Presenter: John Webb
Research: Laura Byrne
Watch the trailer


Script:


Greener on the Other Side
VO: This is Thomas Mnguni. In another life, he might be spending his mornings preparing for an office job. But, instead, a sense of commitment to his community and what he feels is an assault on their human rights bring him here: Emalahleni. It’s the heartland of what some are calling a health crisis.

Thomas Mnguni Upsound in car: CLIP: PETE7711.MOV [00:24] you’ve got a lot of retired people and a lot of youth which is unemployed...

VO: Ferrobank sits alongside Emalahleni, previously Witbank, and is blighted by many of the social problems you find elsewhere in South Africa. But, there’s something else… this is coal burning country. In 2013, it was labelled the dirtiest city in the world. Not because of the state of its streets, but rather the quality of its air.

Thomas Mnguni ITV [03:22] you go into a community meeting, there are maybe 50, 60 people. And then people will say no I’m fine [cough cough]. They keep coughing. So diseases like bronchitis, asthma, consistent coughing – it’s been kind of normalised in these communities.

Jan Sibiya ITV STRAP: “Ferrobank Resident” [05:22] yes. When we wake up in the morning, you see I’ve got these white tiles. They are covered with the black dust when we clean it. You can fill a coffee cup, you can fill it with that dust. It’s too much.

VO: Family man, Jan Sibiya is Ferrobank born and bred but it’s now the last place he wants to be.

Jan Sibiya ITV [05:14] I don’t know what can I say. If I was rich enough I would go and buy a house somewhere and leave this place.

VO: This place isn’t short of coal-related anecdotes. Few, if any, are positive. Not in the poorer communities, anyway.

George Jacobs ITV STRAP “Ferrobank Resident” [00:35] the visibility, especially in the mornings. It becomes so poor that you’ve got to slow down, you’ve got to start looking out for, becoming worried about causing an accident whilst driving or something.

VO: Years of living here have turned George Jacobs into a fatalist. He feels trapped.

George Jacobs ITV [03:22] you are just inclined to keep quiet. What can we do? I can’t take a rope and hang myself to avoid inhaling this dirty air around me. So we live with it.

Thomas Mnguni STRAP “Community Activist, Groundwork” [01:01] we have a government which is supposed to protect the rights of the people – these are basic human rights, we are not asking them to do something extraordinary.

VO: To ensure pollution doesn’t exceed acceptable levels in places like Ferrobank we have what are known as the Minimum Emission Standards or MES. Critics say the standards aren’t strict enough and government appears less than enthusiastic about enforcing even those.

Melita Steele ITV NO STRAP LINE [09:56:01] If you ask me is there political will to act on this problem at the moment my answer would be no.

VO: And nowhere is that lack of political will better demonstrated, says Greenpeace Africa’s Melita Steele, than in government’s handling of Eskom.

Melita Steele ITV [09:59:03] compliance with our minimum emissions standards is – it should be a no brainer. It should be the minimum. We should actually have much stricter standards if we were actually serious about protecting people’s health.

VO: But lenient standards are only half the problem. In 2014 Eskom successfully applied to postpone having to comply with those Minimum Emission Standards for its existing power stations.
Government argues that postponements are legally provided for as a “transitional measure towards compliance”.

That’ll come as little consolation to people familiar with one of pollution’s prime suspects: a gas called Nitrogen Dioxide

Melita Steele ITV STRAP “Greenpeace Africa” [09:48:52] Why is NO2 so bad? Because it’s a dangerous pollutant that damages people’s health specifically in terms of their respiratory systems and when there’s acute exposure it can lead to heart disease and lung cancer.

VO: Chances are, if you live in a city or town, you’re inhaling some right now. That’s because its emitted by vehicle exhausts. But, says Steele, there’s an even bigger culprit.

Melita Steele ITV [09:48:25] According to our analysis, transport and electricity are the worst contributors. But in SA it’s very clear that the air pollution is significantly, primarily, coming from the coal fired power stations.

VO: And that should be of particular concern when you learn that our standard for Nitrogen Dioxide, for example, is 10 times higher than China and Japan’s.

Thomas Mnguni ITV [01:32] So I think this is where our government becomes faulty and this is where we say they intentionally violate people’s rights when it should be a priority for them to protect their basic human rights.

It’s a common spectacle: industry and government entrenched on one side, civil society on the other. If only there was another way…
Well, as it happens there are some shining lights in the global struggle against pollution; countries embracing energy that’s cleaner and greener.

LINK: You’d battle to find a country that takes renewable energy as seriously as Sweden does: it plans to be completely fossil-fuel free within the next ten to fifteen years (20). And, when it comes to the transition to a cleaner future there’s a city tucked away in the south of the country that is… well, a little obsessive.

VO: It’s called Vaxjo, a five hour, 420km drive south of the capital, Stockholm.
With a population size to Emalahleni’s, it’s like many other cities in Scandinavia this time of year: picturesque and covered in snow. But there are things happening here that make it quite unique.

Henrik Johansson ITV STRAP “Environmental Controller, Vaxjo“ [00:02:38] We call ourselves the greenest city in Europe. That is the vision something that we really, really want to achieve.

VO: It may be self-proclaimed, but the title of Europe’s greenest city is entirely deserved. Vaxjo’s even more ambitious than the rest of Sweden and intends ending its reliance on fossil fuels in just over ten years. The impact on damaging pollutants including Nitrogen Dioxide has been significant.

LINK: Henrik Johansonn travels to work from his home here on the outskirts of Vaxjo. Sometimes he takes his car, which is electric, but more-often-than-not he uses his bike. You could say, he’s the greenest citizen in the greenest city in Europe.

VO: And that’s saying something…

VO: This is a city of green energy enthusiasts; of recyclers and re-users. Even the busses here run on food waste.

Henrik Johansson ITV [00:01:23] we have been able to see that if we really want to do something and if we work together among, between different political parties or together with local companies and universities and organizations, we get results and we see the benefits of the results.

VO: But community cooperation can only get you so far. Vaxjo has certain attributes that have made its green metamorphosis well, a little easier.

Sandvik is the city’s very own combined heat and power station run almost entirely on wood chips and off-cuts from the local timber industry. It’s virtually fossil-fuel free.

VO: This plant produces more than half the city’s electricity, and as much as 85% of its heat. The impact has been nothing short of extraordinary.

VO: This graph shows that within 28 years, pollutants like Nitrogen Dioxide have been reduced to levels that make them hardly worth mentioning. Things are not yet perfect, but a future free of fossil fuels is within touching distance.

Henrik Johansson ITV [00:06:06] If we take all energy use altogether including energy for transport 65% is renewable. And that includes transport.

LINK: Take a breath here and what you’re filling your lungs with is some Europe’s cleanest air. So, if Vaxjo occupies one end of the energy extreme – what do cities on the opposite end look like? Well, in SA, you don’t have to travel too far for an answer.

VO: As it turns out, a short drive from Johannesburg. Back to Emalahleni and the province of Mpumalanga. Last year, Greenpeace analysed 3-months-worth of satellite data over the province. Once again, out prime suspect, Nitrogen Dioxide, made an appearance.

Melita Steele ITV [09:47:26] what we can see is that Mpumalanga is the worst NO2 pollution hotspot in the world and the reason for that is because of Eskom’s coal fired power stations in the area.

VO: (Graphic) In response to questions from us, Eskom criticised the Greenpeace report for its focus on pollution from power stations above vehicle emissions. Eskom said its power stations in the Highveld mostly comply with MES, and that emissions of nitrogen oxides at ground level meet the National Ambient Air Quality standards. Eskom acknowledged that emissions from its power stations could lead to negative health impacts, but said it is actively working to reduce its environmental impact.

Steele maintains the impact is being underestimated.

Melita Steele ITV [09:55:16] The really interesting and quite sobering findings of the satellite data is that this air pollution is blown across into Johannesburg and Pretoria. For about 30% of the year we’re exposed to these levels of NO2 pollution.

VO: It’s a stark contrast to places rapidly winning the battle against coal fired power. Places with enviable green ambitions.

LINK: So, what is Vaxjo’s secret: well, some of it is down to luck. There’s also healthy dose of political will and, perhaps most importantly, community buy-in. It seems the Swedes understand better than most the consequences of doing nothing.

ITV Magnus Wohlin STRAP “Vaxjo Sustainability Commission” [[00:09:45] Discussions, discussions, discussions and listening to the people are living in the town. That's the main success formula.

VO: Local politician, Magnus Wohlin, recognises the political risk that comes with enforcing change.

ITV Magnus Wohlin [00:11:59] If you have the people with us there will also be a courage among their politicians to really do the hard transitions, because it's gonna be hard. It's gonna be really difficult to to make this world livable in a hundred years.

VO: But South Africa is not Sweden and Emalahleni is not Vaxjo. However, what led to success in one might just hold lessons for the other: dealing directly with communities at the coalface.

ITV Thomas Mnguni [01:15] Talk right now is about the just transition. We need a fair change. We need to make sure that even if we change from coal to renewables, still people should be at the centre of that change. It shouldn’t be industries

Ends.

Well, in SA, you don’t have to travel too far for an answer. VO: As it turns out, a short drive from Johannesburg. Back to Emalahleni and the province of Mpumalanga. Last year, Greenpeace analysed 3-months-worth of satellite data over the province. Once again, out prime suspect, Nitrogen Dioxide, made an appearance. Places with enviable green ambitions. LINK: So, what is Vaxjo’s secret: well, some of it is down to luck. There’s also healthy dose of political will and, perhaps most importantly, community buy-in. It seems the Swedes understand better than most the consequences of doing nothing. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We travel to Europe's greenest city and ask: What's stopping South Africa's towns from cleaning up their act?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Sweden's Vaxjo claims to be Europe's greenest city. It is carbon neutral, runs its transport network on recycled waste and uses the latest construction techniques to limit the environmental impact of its own expansion. This will be a first-hand view of the type of future all cities should aspire to, and provides the prefect yardstick against which to measure South Africa's cities and towns.
metadata.Summary: This is a story about the type of green future that is possible with a little foresight, planning and political will. Vaxjo is a shining light in a country that has made clear its intention to unburden itself of fossil fuels within the next few years. So precise has its vision become, that it even takes steps to mitigate the environmental impact of modern construction methods. We will be taken on a tour of the city and shown the initiatives and technologies that have made it Europe's greenest. But, this is also a story about a country that is being left behind in the race for carbon neutrality. South Africa is still largely reliant on fossil fuels and one of its provinces holds the inglorious title as the world's most polluted. Recent satellite imagery highlighted alarming levels of Nitrogen Di Oxide in the atmosphere - a direct consequence of the province's positioning at the centre of coal-fired energy provision. It is the antithesis of Vaxjo. Vested interests, misunderstanding, misdirection and fear have all contributed to a widespread distrust of clean energy and its independent producers. So, can South Africa produce its own Vaxjo? And, if not, what will the consequence be of a failure to convince Eskom, the mines and the unions that this is the only way forward?
